text: Maryon Lane (15 February 1931 – 13 June 2008) was a South African ballet dancer who gained prominence in Britain as a ballerina with the Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet and as a soloist with the Royal Ballet. Born Patricia Mills in Zululand, a district of Natal province (now KwaZulu-Natal) on the Indian Ocean coast of South Africa, she moved to Johannesburg, in the northern province of Transvaal (now Gauteng), at around 13 years old in 1944. There, she studied ballet with leading teachers, including Marjorie Sturman, a specialist in the Cecchetti method, and Reina Berman, who had trained in the Cecchetti method before transitioning to the Royal Academy of Dancing (RAD) syllabus. In 1946, shortly after the end of World War II, Mills emigrated to the UK, winning an RAD scholarship to attend the Sadler's Wells Ballet School in London. After one year of study, she joined the corps of the Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet, at which point she adopted her professional name, Maryon Lane, to distinguish herself from another South African dancer named Patricia Miller. The Sadler's Wells Theatre Ballet was a small, young company founded by Ninette de Valois to develop dancers and choreographers following the relocation of the parent company to the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden. Due to the need to replace depleted leading dancers, Lane advanced quickly through the ranks; by 1948, at age 17, she became a principal dancer and performed in major works by de Valois and Frederick Ashton. Petite, with dark hair, a pretty oval face, and ideal proportions, she was noted for her vivid personality, strong technique, and natural musicality. De Valois regarded her as the ideal repertory dancer—capable of demi-caractère and dramatic roles as well as classical work. Throughout her career, she was celebrated for her musicality, attack, and commanding stage presence. She excelled in lighthearted roles such as Swanilda in Coppélia, Lise in Ashton's La Fille Mal Gardée, and the title roles in John Cranko's Pineapple Poll and Léonide Massine's Mam'zelle Angot, as well as in dramatic roles like the vapid Ballerina in Petrushka, the Betrayed Girl in The Rake's Progress, and the adulterous, runaway Bride in Blood Wedding. She was particularly praised for her performance in the demanding fairy variations in the prologue to The Sleeping Beauty and as Princess Aurora. Her most significant contribution was her involvement in creating new ballets, especially those by the young Kenneth MacMillan. In 1955, MacMillan cast her in a principal role in Danses Concertantes, set to Stravinsky’s score with designs by Nicholas Georgiadis, a work that led de Valois to transfer both the ballet and Lane to the main company at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden. She concluded her performing career there as a soloist in 1968. Among the roles she created were several new productions. She was married to Royal Ballet colleague David Blair, with whom she had twin daughters in 1960. In 1961, Blair was promoted to Margot Fonteyn’s regular partner but was soon overshadowed by Rudolf Nureyev’s arrival in 1962. Both Lane and Blair, along with other leading dancers, fell into relative obscurity amid the growing fame of Fonteyn and Nureyev. After leaving the Royal Ballet in 1968, she made occasional guest appearances with London Festival Ballet, Ballet Rambert, and her former company. She then dedicated herself to teaching, becoming an inspired and influential instructor at the London Ballet Centre, and later taught at the Royal Ballet and Ballet Rambert schools and with other companies and seminars. In middle age, after her husband died in 1976, she moved to Cyprus, a former British stronghold in the eastern Mediterranean, settling in the Greek Cypriot town of Kyrenia, a cultural hub and tourist destination on the northern coast. There, she founded the Maryon Lane Ballet Academy. After teaching local students for several years, she passed away in 2008 at the age of 77.
